settings.definition_quote: An adversarial bandit problem is specified by the number K of possible actions ... and by an assignment of rewards, i.e., an infinite sequence x(1), x(2), ... of vectors x(t) = (x1(t), ..., xK(t)), where xi(t) ∈ [0, 1] ... We assume that the player knows the number K of actions.

settings.name_in_paper: adversarial bandit problem (weak regret), known horizon T
settings.definition_quote: Theorem 6.3. For any fixed T > 0, for all K ≥ 2 and for all δ > 0, if γ = min{3/5, 2 sqrt(3/5 K ln K / T)} and α = 2 sqrt(ln(KT/δ)) ...

settings.name_in_paper: K-armed bandit with random reward distribution depending on K and T (lower bound)
unmapped: good arm chosen uniformly at random; regret measured against realized best-arm return Gmax and averaged over the random instance
settings.definition_quote: one action I is chosen uniformly at random to be the 'good' action. The T rewards xI(t) associated with the good action are chosen independently at random to be 1 with probability 1/2 + ǫ and 0 otherwise ... The rewards xj(t) associated with the other actions j ≠ I are chosen independently at random to be 0 or 1 with equal odds.

settings.name_in_paper: adversarial bandit problem with N experts
unmapped: the family of experts must include the uniform expert (or have it in its convex hull)
settings.definition_quote: Formally, an expert i is an infinite sequence ξ^i(1), ξ^i(2), ... ∈ [0,1]^K of probability vectors ... An adversarial bandit problem with N experts is thus specified by both an assignment of rewards to actions and by an assignment of probability vectors to each expert.

settings.name_in_paper: regret against arbitrary sequences of actions (hardness h)
settings.definition_quote: The hardness of a sequence (j1, ..., jT) is defined by h(j1, ..., jT) = 1 + |{1 ≤ ℓ < T : jℓ ≠ jℓ+1}|.

settings.name_in_paper: regret against arbitrary sequences of actions, known T
settings.definition_quote: Corollary 8.2. Assume that algorithm Exp3.S is run with input parameters α = 1/T and γ = min{1, sqrt(K ln(KT)/T)}.

settings.name_in_paper: regret against sequences of hardness at most S, known T and S
unmapped: learner knows a bound S on the hardness h = 1 + number of switches of the comparator sequence
settings.definition_quote: Corollary 8.3 ... holds for any sequence j^T = (j1, ..., jT) of actions such that h(j^T) ≤ S.

settings.name_in_paper: regret against sequences of hardness at most S, known S, unknown T
unmapped: learner knows a bound S on the hardness h = 1 + number of switches of the comparator sequence
settings.definition_quote: Corollary 8.5 ... for any T > 0 and for any sequence j^T = (j1, ..., jT) of actions such that h(j^T) ≤ S.

settings.name_in_paper: unknown game setup (repeated N-person game, payoffs in [0,1])
unmapped: rewards are payoffs of a repeated game chosen by other players adaptively
settings.definition_quote: this corresponds to assuming that the vector (x1(t), ..., xK(t)) of rewards for each trial t is chosen by an adversary who knows the gambler's strategy and the outcome of the gambler's random draws up to time t − 1.

settings.out_of_scope_reason: Game-theoretic guarantee: per-round payoff relative to the game value v of an unknown matrix game
unmapped: entries of M in known interval [a,b]
guarantee is relative to the minimax value v, not regret
settings.definition_quote: Let M be an unknown game matrix in [a, b]^{n×m} with value v. Suppose the row player, knowing only a, b, and n, uses the mixed strategy Exp3.1.

symbols.G_max: return of the best single action up to T

source.quote: For any K > 0 and for any γ ∈ (0, 1], Gmax − E[GExp3] ≤ (e − 1)γGmax + K ln K/γ holds for any assignment of rewards and for any T > 0.

results.notes: Rewards fixed in advance (oblivious), so Gmax - E[G] is expected regret against best fixed action.

symbols.g: known upper bound on G_max used for tuning

conditions: g >= G_max is known to the learner
tuning: gamma = min{1, sqrt(K ln K / ((e-1) g))}

source.quote: For any T > 0, assume that g ≥ Gmax and that algorithm Exp3 is run with input parameter γ = min{1, sqrt(K ln K/((e − 1)g))}. Then Gmax − E[GExp3] ≤ 2 sqrt(e − 1) sqrt(gK ln K) ≤ 2.63 sqrt(gK ln K) holds for any assignment of rewards.

results.notes: Learner needs g (not in vocabulary); with known T one may take g = T giving 2 sqrt(e-1) sqrt(TK ln K). Horizon marked 'known' since an a priori bound g is needed.

symbols.G_max: return of the best single action up to T

source.quote: For any K > 0, Gmax − E[GExp3.1] ≤ 8 sqrt(e − 1) sqrt(Gmax K ln K) + 8(e − 1)K + 2K ln K ≤ 10.5 sqrt(Gmax K ln K) + 13.8 K + 2K ln K holds for any assignment of rewards and for any T > 0.

results.notes: Holds uniformly over T. Theorem 9.3 applies this to unknown matrix games.

source.quote: For any number of actions K ≥ 2 and for any time horizon T, there exists a distribution over the assignment of rewards such that the expected weak regret of any algorithm (where the expectation is taken with respect to both the randomization over rewards and the algorithm's internal randomization) is at least (1/20) min{sqrt(KT), T}.

results.notes: Regret is E[Gmax - G_A] with Gmax the realized best return; instance depends on T and K. Implies the same lower bound for the adversarial setting.

symbols.eps_lb: bias epsilon in (0,1/2] of the good arm in the lower-bound construction

source.quote: For any player strategy A, and for the distribution on rewards described above, the expected regret of algorithm A is lower bounded by E∗[Gmax − GA] ≥ ǫ(T − T/K − (T/2) sqrt(−(T/K) ln(1 − 4ǫ²))).

results.notes: Bracket placement reconstructed from the proof (E*[G_A] <= T/2 + eps(T/K + (T/2)sqrt(-(T/K)ln(1-4eps^2)))); text extraction was lossy.

tuning: gamma = min{3/5, 2 sqrt(3/5 * K ln K / T)}

source.quote: For any fixed T > 0, for all K ≥ 2 and for all δ > 0, if γ = min{3/5, 2 sqrt(3/5 K ln K/T)} and α = 2 sqrt(ln(KT/δ)), then Gmax − GExp3.P ≤ 4 sqrt(KT ln(KT/δ)) + 4 sqrt(5/3 KT ln K) + 8 ln(KT/δ) holds for any assignment of rewards with probability at least 1 − δ.

results.notes: Realized weak regret bound with probability >= 1-delta over the algorithm's randomization.

bound.regime: T >= 2^{r*}, r* = min{r : delta_r >= K T_r exp(-K T_r)}

tuning: Exp3.P restarted on epochs T_r = 2^r with delta_r = delta/((r+1)(r+2)) and parameters as in Theorem 6.3

source.quote: Let r∗ be as in (24). Let K ≥ 2, δ ∈ (0, 1), and T ≥ 2^{r∗}. Let cT = 2 ln(2 + log2 T). Then Gmax − GExp3.P.1 ≤ 10/(√2−1) sqrt(2KT (ln(KT/δ) + cT)) + 10(1 + log2 T)(ln(KT/δ) + cT) holds with probability at least 1 − δ.

results.notes: Placement of c_T inside the square root reconstructed from lossy PDF text and the proof. Corollary 6.5 (almost-sure: (Gmax - G)/sqrt(T ln T f(T)) -> 0 for any f -> infinity) follows and is not recorded separately.

symbols.G_tilde_max: expected return of the best expert, max_i sum_t xi^i(t)·x(t)

conditions: the family of experts includes the uniform expert (or it lies in their convex hull)

source.quote: For any K, T > 0, for any γ ∈ (0, 1], and for any family of experts which includes the uniform expert, G̃max − E[GExp4] ≤ (e − 1)γ G̃max + K ln N/γ holds for any assignment of rewards.

results.notes: Tuning gamma with g >= G̃max gives O(sqrt(gK ln N)) as remarked in text.

symbols.h: hardness of comparator sequence j^T: 1 + number of switches

source.quote: For any K > 0, for any γ ∈ (0, 1], and for any α > 0, G_{j^T} − E[GExp3.S] ≤ K(h(j^T) ln(K/α) + eαT)/γ + (e − 1)γT holds for any assignment of rewards, for any T > 0, and for any sequence j^T = (j1, ..., jT) of actions.

results.notes: Regret against arbitrary fixed sequence of actions with hardness h; h = S_T + 1.

symbols.h: hardness of comparator sequence j^T: 1 + number of switches

source.quote: Assume that algorithm Exp3.S is run with input parameters α = 1/T and γ = min{1, sqrt(K ln(KT)/T)}. Then G_{j^T} − E[GExp3.S] ≤ h(j^T) sqrt(KT ln(KT)) + 2e sqrt(KT/ln(KT)) holds for any sequence j^T = (j1, ..., jT) of actions.

symbols.S_h: known upper bound S on the hardness h(j^T) (= 1 + switches)

conditions: comparator sequence has hardness h(j^T) <= S_h

source.quote: Assume that algorithm Exp3.S is run with input parameters α = 1/T and γ = min{1, sqrt(K(S ln(KT) + e)/((e − 1)T))}. Then G_{j^T} − E[GExp3.S] ≤ 2 sqrt(e − 1) sqrt(KT(S ln(KT) + e)) holds for any sequence j^T of actions such that h(j^T) ≤ S.

results.notes: Paper's S is a hardness bound, not a parameter norm; renamed S_h.

symbols.h: hardness of comparator sequence j^T: 1 + number of switches

tuning: Exp3.S restarted on epochs T_r = 2^r with parameters of Corollary 8.2

source.quote: G_{j^T} − E[GExp3.S.1] ≤ (h(j^T) + 2e)/(√2 − 1) sqrt(2KT ln(KT)) for any T > 0 and for any sequence j^T = (j1, ..., jT) of actions.

results.notes: Doubling-trick version, no knowledge of T.

symbols.S_h: known upper bound S on the hardness h(j^T) (= 1 + switches)

conditions: comparator sequence has hardness h(j^T) <= S_h
tuning: Exp3.S restarted on epochs T_r = 2^r with parameters of Corollary 8.3

source.quote: G_{j^T} − E[GExp3.S.1] ≤ 2 sqrt(e − 1)/(√2 − 1) sqrt(2KT(S ln(KT) + e)) for any T > 0 and for any sequence j^T = (j1, ..., jT) of actions such that h(j^T) ≤ S.

If player i has K ≥ 2 pure strategies and plays in the unknown game setup (with payoffs in [0, 1]) using the mixed strategy Exp3.P.1, then max_{j∈Si} R_i^(j)(T) ≤ 10/(√2−1) sqrt(2K/T (ln(KT/δ) + cT)) + 10(1 + log2 T)/T (ln(KT/δ) + cT), where cT = 2 ln(2 + log2 T), holds with probability at least 1 − δ, for all 0 < δ < 1 and for all T ≥ (ln(K/δ))^{1/(K−1)}.

results.notes: Bound is on the AVERAGE (per-round) regret R_i(T) = (1/T) sum, against an adaptive adversary (other players). Corollary 9.2 (Hannan consistency) follows; not recorded.

conditions: game matrix M in [a,b]^{n x m}
row player knows a, b and n (number of rows = K)

source.quote: Let M be an unknown game matrix in [a, b]^{n×m} with value v. Suppose the row player, knowing only a, b, and n, uses the mixed strategy Exp3.1. Then the row player's expected payoff per round is at least v − 8(b − a)(sqrt(e−1) sqrt(n ln n/T) − 8(e − 1) n/T − 2 n ln n/T).

results.notes: Recorded as an upper bound on v minus expected per-round payoff. The printed expression is garbled by PDF extraction; reconstructed from the proof (vT − 8√(e−1)√(Tn ln n) − 8(e−1)n − 2n ln n, for [a,b]=[0,1]), with (b−a) scaling applied to all terms. The paper's n (number of rows) is K.
